section_1.title: Introduction: Fermat's Principle
section_1.content: Introduce Fermat's Principle of Least Time. Light chooses the path that takes the minimum time to travel between two points. Connect this to an intuitive real-world scenario.
section_1.example: A lifeguard on a beach needs to reach a drowning swimmer in the water as quickly as possible. Since they run faster on sand than they swim in water, they don't move in a straight line; they choose an angled path to minimize total travel time.

section_2.title: Geometric Setup and Variables
section_2.content: Define the interface between two media (n1, n2). Use a diagram to show light traveling from point A to point B, crossing at distance 'x' along the boundary. Define angles of incidence (θ1) and refraction (θ2) relative to the normal.
section_2.example: Visual animation showing two medium layers: 'Medium 1 (Air)' and 'Medium 2 (Glass)'. A coordinate system overlays the interface, showing the horizontal displacement x and the fixed vertical depths d1 and d2.

section_3.title: Formulating the Time Equation
section_3.content: Express total time T as a function of path lengths and velocities: T(x) = (sqrt(d1^2 + x^2) / v1) + (sqrt(d2^2 + (L-x)^2) / v2). Emphasize that finding the path of least time requires minimizing this function.
section_3.example: An animation slider moving point 'x' back and forth along the interface, updating the total time calculation in real-time to show that only one specific 'x' results in the minimum time.

section_4.title: Calculus: Finding the Minimum
section_4.content: Take the derivative dT/dx and set it to zero. Using the chain rule, derive the relationship between geometry and velocity: sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2. Relate velocity to the refractive index (n = c/v).
section_4.example: Step-by-step mathematical derivation appearing alongside a dynamic geometric plot that visualizes d(sinθ)/dx.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Snell's Law
section_5.content: Substitute n = c/v into the derived equation to arrive at the final form: n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2). Summarize how physics and calculus converge to predict light behavior.
section_5.example: The final formula glows in the center of the screen, followed by a quick visual application: a laser pointer hitting a glass block, with the angles matching the formula perfectly.
